questions.q: List the seven features of Multinational Corporations as described in the NCERT Class 11 Business Studies textbook.
questions.a: The seven features are: (i) Huge capital resources, (ii) Foreign collaboration, (iii) Advanced technology, (iv) Product innovation, (v) Marketing strategies, (vi) Expansion of market territory, (vii) Centralised control. A wrong answer (e.g., listing only 3-4 features or confusing with joint venture features like "shared ownership") reveals the student has memorised a partial list or conflates MNCs with other global enterprise forms.

questions.q: Explain why 'centralised control' is a distinguishing feature of MNCs compared to a contractual joint venture.
questions.a: In an MNC, the headquarters in the home country sets broad policy frameworks for all subsidiaries worldwide, while day-to-day operations are decentralised. In a contractual joint venture, there is no separate legal entity; control is shared through agreement without a unified global hierarchy. A wrong answer (e.g., "both have centralised control" or "joint ventures have centralised control") shows the student cannot differentiate between hierarchical global control (MNC) and contractual shared control (JV).

questions.q: A company 'GlobalTech Inc.' is headquartered in Germany. It has a subsidiary in India that manufactures smartphones using German technology, sources components from Vietnam, and sells in 50 countries. The Indian subsidiary follows broad pricing and branding guidelines from Germany but manages daily production locally. Identify which features of MNCs are exhibited in this scenario.
questions.a: Features exhibited: (1) Huge capital resources (global sourcing, multi-country ops), (2) Foreign collaboration (tech from Germany, components from Vietnam), (3) Advanced technology (German tech in production), (4) Product innovation (smartphones), (5) Marketing strategies (global branding), (6) Expansion of market territory (50 countries), (7) Centralised control (broad guidelines from Germany). Missing any feature or misattributing (e.g., saying "shared ownership" for centralised control) indicates inability to map textbook features to real-world operations.

questions.q: Compare the capital structure and funding sources of an MNC entering India with a Government Company (as per Companies Act 2013) in the same sector.
questions.a: An MNC raises capital globally: equity, debentures, bonds, loans from international banks, and host-country investors, leveraging its global credibility. A Government Company gets ≥51% paid-up capital from Central/State Government, with remaining from private shareholders; it can also raise funds from capital markets but relies heavily on government equity. A wrong answer (e.g., "both rely on government funding" or "MNCs only use home country capital") shows confusion between MNCs' global financial reach and Government Companies' state-dependent capital.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The entry of MNCs in the Indian retail sector will benefit consumers but harm small domestic retailers in the long run." Justify with two merits and two limitations of MNCs.
questions.a: Merits supporting consumer benefit: (1) Advanced technology and efficient supply chains lower costs and prices; (2) Aggressive marketing and product innovation increase choice and quality. Limitations harming small retailers: (1) Huge capital and marketing power create unfair competition, driving small players out; (2) Profit repatriation reduces domestic capital accumulation. A one-sided answer (only merits or only limitations) reveals inability to weigh competing impacts — a key analytical skill for board exams.

questions.q: Design a hypothetical entry strategy for a European electric vehicle MNC entering India, incorporating at least four MNC features. Explain how each feature shapes the strategy.
questions.a: Strategy: (1) Huge capital: Invest ₹10,000 cr via equity and green bonds for a Gujarat plant. (2) Advanced technology: Transfer battery management system from German R&D centre. (3) Product innovation: Launch India-specific affordable EV model with localised features. (4) Centralised control: Global HQ sets quality/safety standards; Indian subsidiary handles production/sales. (5) Marketing: Leverage global brand with localised campaigns. A poor answer lists generic steps without linking to MNC features (e.g., "advertise heavily" without mentioning global brand leverage), showing lack of conceptual integration.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A ______ Corporation (MNC) is a large industrial organisation that extends its industrial and marketing operations through a network of branches, subsidiaries, and affiliates in several countries, with centralised control from its headquarters in the home country, characterised by huge capital resources, advanced technology, foreign collaboration, product innovation, aggressive marketing strategies, and global market territory expansion.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you walk into a shopping mall and see a Samsung ______, a Nike shoe, and a Coca-Cola bottle.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can list and explain all seven distinguishing features of MNCs, evaluate their merits and limitations for a host country like India using specific examples, and differentiate MNCs from joint ventures and public sector enterprises based on ownership, control, and operational scope.
